chapters.title: Book One: Resistance - Defining the Enemy
chapters.sourcePressure: The source sidecar supports Resistance as invisible, recurring, and strongest around real work; it ties calling to intensified avoidance and includes the Hitler-in-Vienna anecdote only as a severe example of Resistance beating a would-be artist.
chapters.coreMove: Name the reasonable-sounding delay that appears at the threshold of meaningful work as Resistance before trusting it as caution.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating Resistance as ordinary procrastination, low motivation, or a general need for better time management.

chapters.title: Book Two: Combating Resistance - Turning Pro
chapters.sourcePressure: The source sidecar supports the shift from studying the war to practicing it, with turning pro as the governing move: routine, standards, patience, and impersonal commitment against Resistance.
chapters.coreMove: Transfer authority from mood to a kept work appointment so Resistance cannot renegotiate the labor each day.
chapters.commonMisread: Saying the answer is to grind harder, chase discipline for its own sake, or wait for a perfect productivity system.

chapters.title: Book Three: Beyond Resistance - The Higher Realm
chapters.sourcePressure: The source sidecar supports a move beyond Resistance and turning pro into a larger creative or spiritual duty, using higher-realm and Muse language only narrowly and keeping the frame practical, bounded, and tied to craft.
chapters.coreMove: Let the work itself, not ego or approval hunger, become the authority that shapes the final choices.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning the higher realm into vague mysticism, chosen-artist theater, or permission to ignore craft standards.
